q: Heat engine is a system that converts heat to mechanical energy, which can then be used to do mechanical work.
e: True. It repeats a cycle so work keeps coming out. Turning work into heat is dissipation, not this engine. A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so it can do mechanical work.

q: Heat engine is a system that converts mechanical energy to heat energy, which can then be used to do thermal work.
e: False. A heat engine converts heat into mechanical energy so that mechanical work can be delivered. The opposite direction is closer to a mechanical dissipater. Cycle after cycle, work is the output.

q: A series of processes in which a system is brought back to its initial state is called a cycle.
e: True. A cycle is a series of processes that returns the system to its initial state. Net Delta U over a cycle is zero. Then W equals Q_H minus Q_C for a heat engine.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of work output to heat input.
e: True. Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H. You can also write 1 - Q_C/Q_H. Heat input over work output is the reciprocal, not the efficiency.

q: Thermal efficiency for a heat engine is the ratio of heat input to work output.
e: False. Thermal efficiency is work output over heat input, W/Q_H, not the reciprocal. A ratio bigger than 1 would claim more work than the heat you paid. The leftover heat is Q_C.

q: Applying the first law of thermodynamic to one complete cycle, remembering that there is no net change of internal energy ($\Delta U = 0$), we get, $Q_H - Q_C = W$.
e: True. For an ideal gas it depends only on absolute temperature. Heat and work can change U but are not stored as heat or work. Internal energy U is the total microscopic energy of the particles.

q: The transformation of heat into work is usually accomplished in practice by two general types of engine; the internal combustion engine and the steam engine.
e: True. In both, a gas in a cylinder is taken around a cycle. Nuclear or solar plants are different textbook chapters. Practical heat-into-work machines are internal combustion engines and steam engines.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place explosively by an electric spark.
e: True. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. A gasoline engine ignites the fuel-air mix with an electric spark. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust.

q: In the gasoline engines, the combustion of the gasoline and air takes place slowly by compression heat alone.
e: False. In a gasoline engine the mixture explodes from an electric spark, not from compression heat alone. Slow compression ignition is the diesel idea. Gasoline needs that spark at the end of the compression stroke.

q: The cycle involves the performance of six processes, of which four require motion of the piston and are called strokes.
e: True. A gas confined by a piston in a cylinder is the usual thermodynamic system. Heat in, work out, and U can all be tracked on that cylinder. Strokes are the piston motions in an engine cycle.

q: Intake stroke: A mixture of gasoline vapour and air is drawn into the cylinder by the suction stroke of the piston.
e: True. Diesel intake draws air only. Compression then raises p and T of whatever was drawn in. On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air.

q: Compression stroke: The mixture of gasoline vapour and air is compressed until its pressure and temperature rise considerably.
e: True. The compression stroke squeezes the charge until pressure and temperature rise sharply. Gasoline then waits for a spark; diesel waits for injected fuel. Volume falls; p and T climb.

q: Explosion: Combustion of the hot mixture is caused to take place very rapidly by an electric spark.
e: True. Gasoline combustion is a rapid spark explosion at nearly constant volume; the piston barely moves in that instant. Pressure jumps, then the power stroke expands the hot gases. Diesel ignition is compression heat plus injection, not that spark pop.

q: Power stroke: The hot combustion products expand and push the piston out, thus suffering a drop in pressure and temperature.
e: True. That is the work-delivery leg. Exhaust then dumps what is left. On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature.

q: Valve exhaust: The combustion products at the end of the power stroke are still at a higher pressure and temperature than the outside.
e: True. Exhaust then dumps what is left. On the power stroke the hot gases expand, push the piston, and drop in pressure and temperature. That is the work-delivery leg.

q: Exhaust stroke: The piston pushes almost all the remaining combustion products out of the cylinder.
e: True. They still leave hotter and at higher pressure than the outside. A slightly larger push than outside pressure is needed to empty the cylinder. The exhaust stroke has the piston push remaining combustion products out.

q: The diesel engine operates on either a two-stroke or four-stroke cycle.
e: True. A full cycle has net Delta U = 0, so W = Q_H - Q_C. A diesel draws only air, then sprays fuel that ignites from compression heat and pressure. No spark is required at that instant.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces only air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: True. Four of the six processes are piston strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Diesel instead compresses air only and injects fuel that auto-ignites. On the gasoline intake, or suction, stroke the piston draws in gasoline vapour and air.

q: Unlike the spark-ignition gasoline engine, the diesel engine induces a mixture of fuel and air into the combustion chamber on its intake stroke.
e: False. A diesel draws only air on the intake stroke. Fuel is sprayed in later and ignites from the heat and pressure. The gasoline engine is the one that intakes a fuel-air mixture.

q: Diesel fuel is sprayed into the cylinder by the injector and immediately ignites because of the heat and pressure inside the cylinder.
e: True. Equal temperatures mean zero net heat flow. A diesel draws only air, then sprays fuel that ignites from compression heat and pressure. No spark is required at that instant.

q: In 1824, Nicolas Leonard Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical engine known as Carnot engine.
e: True. In 1824 Sadi Carnot described a hypothetical reversible engine between two reservoirs. That Carnot engine sets the upper efficiency bound for every real engine on the same pair of temperatures. Friction and irreversibility make real engines worse.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an ideal reversible cycle (Carnot cycle) between two heat reservoirs.
e: True. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor. All reversible engines on that pair share the same efficiency. The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs.

q: Carnot engine is a heat engine operates on an irreversible cycle between two heat reservoirs.
e: False. The Carnot engine runs on an ideal reversible cycle between two reservoirs. Irreversibility is what makes real engines worse. Two isotherms and two adiabats, all reversible, make the Carnot loop.

q: Carnot engine sets an upper limit on the efficiency of all other real engines.
e: True. You must use absolute temperatures in eta_c = 1 - T_C/T_H. Real cycles leak heat and generate friction, so they sit below that ceiling. Carnot sets an upper limit on the efficiency of steam, gasoline and diesel engines between the same temperatures.

q: All real engines are less efficient than Carnot engine because they do not operate through a reversible cycle.
e: True. All reversible engines on that pair share the same efficiency. The Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle of two isotherms and two adiabats between two reservoirs. It is an upper limit, not a workshop motor.

q: All real engines are more efficient than Carnot engine because they operate through a reversible cycle.
e: False. Real engines are less efficient than Carnot, because they are not reversible and they lose energy to friction and conduction. Carnot sets the upper bound. Nobody beats that bound between the same two reservoirs.

q: In a reversible process, the system undergoing the process can be returned to its initial condition along the same path on the p-V diagram.
e: True. In a reversible process you can return along the same p-V path to the start. Infinitesimally slow is the main thermodynamic condition. An irreversible process cannot retrace that path.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out infinitesimally slowly.
e: True. The two branches complement each other; they are not unrelated. A reversible process can retrace the same p-V path if you go infinitesimally slowly. Carnot's four legs are all reversible.

q: The most important condition for a process to be reversible in thermodynamics is that the process should be carried out as rapidly as possible.
e: False. Reversibility wants the process carried out infinitesimally slowly, so the system can retrace the same p-V path. Rush it and you leave equilibrium. Rapid is the irreversible direction.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isothermal processes and two adiabatic processes.
e: True. Isothermal means constant temperature, so for an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and W = Q. Heat must leak slowly enough to keep equilibrium. Work is n R T ln(Vf/Vi) for the ideal-gas case.

q: The Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes; two isobaric processes and two isochoric processes.
e: False. The Carnot cycle is two reversible isotherms and two reversible adiabats. Isobaric and isochoric legs belong to other model cycles. Those four Carnot legs are what set the T_C/T_H efficiency.

q: Carnot's theorem states that no engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: True. Carnot's theorem: no engine between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine on those reservoirs. The corollary is that all reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient. Different efficiencies mean irreversibility or different temperatures.

q: Carnot's theorem states that any engine operating between two heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs.
e: False. Carnot's theorem forbids any engine between two reservoirs from beating Carnot on those same reservoirs. More efficient than Carnot would break the second-law bound. Reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient, not wilder.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs are equally efficient.
e: True. The corollary is that all reversible engines on that pair are equally efficient. Different efficiencies mean irreversibility or different temperatures. Carnot's theorem: no engine between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a Carnot engine on those reservoirs.

q: A corollary to Carnot's theorem states that all reversible engines operating between the same heat reservoirs have different efficiencies.
e: False. The corollary is that all reversible engines between the same reservoirs are equally efficient. Different efficiencies would appear only if the engines were irreversible or the reservoirs differed. Carnot's value is shared, not scattered.
